links.outcome: Reading grade level of chatbot concussion advice versus 6th-grade benchmark
links.effect: No chatbot met the 6th-grade level on all measures; most exceeded 10th grade; Perplexity lowest FKGL 7.46; Copilot FKGL 12.55, Gemini 12.97; FRES 27.7–54.2 vs 80–90 target.
links.quote: The overall result was the noncompliance of all five AI platforms: none of them achieved the recommended 6th grade reading level (AMA/CDC standard) in all measures.

links.outcome: Plain-language comprehensibility of AI-generated patient education outputs
links.effect: All five chatbots exceeded 6th-grade level; FKGL and GFI stayed above 10th grade for most; FRES far below the 80–90 plain-English range.
links.quote: Both FKGL and GFI indices maintained the content at both high-school to collegiate reading level (> 10th grade).

links.outcome: Information quality (DISCERN, EQIP) of retrieval-augmented vs pretrained chatbots
links.effect: Perplexity Pro DISCERN 47.36 vs ChatGPT 36.18 and EQIP 65.00 vs 52.73; RAG systems higher than ChatGPT/Gemini (r=0.545–0.638); GQS did not differ (p=0.373).
links.quote: Dunn post hoc testing (Table 2 ) showed that Perplexity Pro scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini on both DISCERN and EQIP ( r = 0.545–0.638), indicating large effect sizes for these comparisons.

links.outcome: Transparency and attribution of chatbot responses via JAMA benchmarks
links.effect: JAMA transparency uniformly low: ChatGPT 0.00, DeepSeek 0.00, Gemini 0.00, Copilot 0.64, Perplexity 1.00 out of 4 (H=40.35, p<0.001).

links.outcome: Output quality against Amsterdam Consensus reference standards via DISCERN, EQIP, GQS
links.effect: Quality varied by model: DISCERN 36.18–47.36, EQIP 52.73–65.00; GQS moderate to good (2.91–3.36) without significant differences (p=0.373).
links.quote: Kruskal–Wallis testing identified significant between-model differences for DISCERN ( H = 20.161, p = 0.0005, η 2 = 0.323), EQIP ( H = 20.432, p = 0.0004, η 2 = 0.329), and JAMA ( H = 40.350, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.727).
